the neuroanatomical alterations in the brain that are present in young people at risk of schizophrenia can be detected using structural MRI and that they may be useful as markers to identify young people at high risk for schizophrenia.

the brains of individuals at high risk for schizophrenia are smaller than the brains of healthy controls and that the brains of high-risk subjects who develop schizophrenia are smaller than those of high-risk subjects that do not develop schizophrenia.

the neuroimaging findings in schizophrenia are not yet sufficiently robust to be used in clinical practice.

the neuroanatomical abnormalities in schizophrenia are not specific for the illness, but are associated with the illness, and that the neuroanatomic abnormalities are not the cause of the illness, but may represent an end result of the illness.

we have shown that the neurodevelopmental hypothesis for schizophrenia is supported by neuroimaging studies.
